name: Yusuf Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Anything you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Harun at Stonebridge, a beef and hay farm, about a hundred and twenty suckler cows, which means cows that raise their own calves, plus eighty hectares of grass and a bit of barley. Mornings I feed round with the old blue tractor and the bale handler, check the cows in the sheds, and see to anything lame or off. Afternoons it's fencing, mucking out, fixing whatever's broken. I like it because I know what each day is going to be.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet. I live with my partner Amira in a rented bungalow two miles from the farm, and she's a receptionist at the vet's in town. We've got about three months of money saved, which we're putting towards a house deposit one day. I don't do much online; I keep my calving records in a paper notebook, and my uncle does the same, which drives the vet mad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, all that fuss for nothing much. I don't really post things online, so it'd be at the livestock mart, probably, chatting at the pens. Most people there would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not surprised. I've never used any of those AI programs and I never needed to. If it all stays the same, I can keep doing what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. Keep working for Harun, keep saving for the deposit, maybe ten or fifteen percent of what I earn each month. I'd probably get the forklift ticket I've been meaning to, because the feed merchant asks for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Just normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep paper records. Has anyone ever pushed you to change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vet, the feed rep, Amira. Amira set me up with an app once, and I used it for about a week and then the phone got dropped in a water trough. The notebook's never been dropped in a trough, or if it has, it dried out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like most about knowing what each day will be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not a surprises person. My dad moved us around a lot for his work when I was a kid, three schools in six years. So a farm where the same cows need the same things every morning suits me.

S0.say: I'd say all that fuss came to nothing much. I don't post online, so I'd say it at the livestock market, chatting by the pens.
S0.think: I'd be relieved but not surprised, because I've never used AI programs and never needed them. If things stay the same, I can keep doing what I know.
S0.do: Carries on working for his uncle and keeps saving ten to fifteen percent of his pay towards a house deposit. Probably gets the forklift certificate the feed merchant asks for.
S0.quote: The notebook's never been dropped in a trough, or if it has, it dried out.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf likes routine and has a personal reason for it: moving schools often as a child. He has tried technology at his partner's urging and let it go without fuss. A plateau simply confirms what he expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change the big places, the arable farms and the big dairies, and leave the small beef men alone mostly. That's what I'd say at the mart, and I think most of them would nod. Things change, you get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be fine for a while. Harun's still running a tractor from 1996 and won't spend money he doesn't have to, so he's not buying a robot any time soon. The thing I'd think about is whether the big farms would make beef cheaper than we can, but that'd take years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and wait to see what the neighbours do. I'm not going to rush into anything. Maybe if Harun asked me to learn something, a new feeder or whatever, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little thought in the back of my head, but not a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the big farms might make beef cheaper. What would happen to Stonebridge if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harun would grumble, then probably cut the herd back and do more hay to sell. He's done it before, when prices fell a few years ago. We got through by not spending, which he's very good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on the farm or nearby you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on our farm, it's just the two of us and a lad in summer. But my friend Callum milks at the big dairy on the hill, three hundred cows, and they've been talking about robots for ages. I'd tell him to keep his eyes open.

S1.say: I'd say it'll change the big arable farms and dairies and mostly leave small beef farms alone. Things change, and you get on with it.
S1.think: I think we'd be fine for a while, because my uncle runs a 1996 tractor and won't buy a robot any time soon. The question is whether big farms make beef cheaper than we can, but that would take years.
S1.do: Keeps working as he is and waits to see what neighbouring farms do. Would learn a new machine only if his uncle asked him to, and wouldn't go looking for training.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small thought at the back of his mind.
S1.quote: Harun's still running a tractor from 1996 and won't spend money he doesn't have to, so he's not buying a robot any time soon.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf sees his small family beef farm as a shelter, mainly because his uncle is so careful with money. He does spot the real risk, cheaper beef from big farms, but places it years away. He'd pass a warning to a friend at a large dairy rather than act himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too quick and the government's got to do something sensible, not panic, not ban it, but help people through. That's what I'd say at the mart. I wouldn't want to be one of those shouting on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one frightens me. If machines can do everything in two years, the big farms with robots could sell beef for half what it costs us, and Harun would have to sell up. And I'd be twenty-nine with nothing on paper except a farm certificate and a forklift ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop saving for the house and keep that money as our safety net instead. I'd talk to Harun about what he'd do and whether there'd be work for me. If the farm went, I'd look for local work with animals, maybe at the vet's with Amira or at the market, and if there was nothing, I'd lean on family, because my parents and Harun would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. Not sleeping well, I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop saving for the house. What does that mean for you and Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means putting off the thing we've been working for, for about four years now. She'd understand, but she'd be sad; she's been looking at houses on her phone every night. I'd hate being the reason we stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new to stay ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd learn. If the machines can do everything, what's the point of me learning computers in my late twenties when the computer can do it better? I'd rather stick with animals and hope there's still somebody wanted to look at a lame cow.

S2.say: I'd say it's too quick and the government should help people through it sensibly, not panic or ban it. I wouldn't be one of those shouting online.
S2.think: This one frightens me, because robot farms could sell beef for half our cost and my uncle would have to sell. I'd be twenty-nine with only a farm certificate and a forklift ticket.
S2.do: Stops saving for the house and keeps the money as a safety net. Talks to his uncle about the farm's future, looks for local animal work at the vet's or the market if the farm goes, and leans on family if nothing turns up.
S2.quote: I'd rather stick with animals and hope there's still somebody wanted to look at a lame cow.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks through Yusuf's calm because it hits the family farm, not just his role. He'd sooner pause the house deposit than retrain, and he doesn't see the point of learning computers if the machines will do it better. His biggest personal sadness is letting Amira down on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government to put a plan together for farming, if they're sensible about it. I'd say it at the mart and at the farmers' meeting at the church hall. I'd also say don't sell your farm in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still bad for us, just slower. Harun would hang on as long as he could, but small beef farms would get squeezed. I'd be thirty-two, and honestly I don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, but I'd hold off on the house until we saw how it was going. I'd ask Harun, maybe in the first year, if he'd think about diversifying, like letting the old barn out or doing farm stays, because people might still want those. I wouldn't do much else until it actually started hitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the two-year one, but there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on the house. How long would you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of years, maybe. If things looked steady by 2029, we'd buy something small. If they didn't, we'd keep renting and keep the money where we can get at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't sell in a panic. Why that, in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when prices fell a few years back, a family down the road sold their land cheap to a big company, and then prices came back up the year after. Harun still talks about it. He says the ones who sit tight usually do better.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible government plan for farming. I'd tell people at the market and the church hall meeting not to sell their farms in a panic.
S3.think: I think it's still bad for us, just slower, because small beef farms would get squeezed. I'd be thirty-two and I honestly don't know what else I'd do.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving but holds off on buying a house for a couple of years. Asks his uncle in the first year about renting out the old barn or doing farm stays, then waits until the change actually starts to bite.
S3.feel: Anxious, though less than with two years.
S3.quote: He says the ones who sit tight usually do better.
S3.fieldNote: Yusuf's response to more time is to wait more carefully, not to act sooner. His caution has a family lesson behind it: a neighbour who sold land cheap just before prices recovered. His one new idea, renting the barn or farm stays, is about the farm rather than about himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd say there's time for everyone to adjust, farmers included. I'd say farms will change like they always have, from horses to tractors and now this. That's what my granddad used to say about the tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, there's a thing I haven't said yet. Harun's got no children, and the plan has always been that Stonebridge comes to me one day. If by 2036 machines can farm better and cheaper, that plan might not be worth much, and that's harder to think about than the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the farm and saving. I'd talk properly with Harun about the farm's future, which we've never really done, probably over a Sunday dinner. We'd go ahead with a small house in a few years, because ten years is too long to wait. I might do a short course at the agricultural college on running a farm business, if Harun was willing to pay half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a slower way. It's the inheritance that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never really talked with Harun about the farm's future. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not done in our family, talking about after someone's gone. He'd change the subject to the weather. But if this was coming, I think I'd have to, even if it's awkward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To know what he wants, really. Whether he'd want me to keep it going as a small farm, sell some land, or put it into something else. I'd rather know now than find out from a lawyer.

S4.say: I'd say ten years gives everyone time to adjust, and farming changes like it always has, from horses to tractors to this. That's what my granddad said about tractors.
S4.think: My uncle has no children and the farm is meant to come to me one day. If machines farm better and cheaper by 2036, that plan might not be worth much, and that's harder to face than losing the job.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and has a proper talk with his uncle over Sunday dinner about the farm's future. Goes ahead with buying a small house in a few years and might take a short farm business course if his uncle pays half.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slower way, mostly about the inheritance.
S4.quote: It's not done in our family, talking about after someone's gone.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture surfaced Yusuf's real stake: he expects to inherit his uncle's farm, and he fears it could lose its value. More time doesn't calm him; it gives the worry room to grow. The only step he'd take early is the hard family conversation he has been avoiding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time and Harun might have to sell before we even understood what was happening. What would help is the government supporting small family farms through it, maybe keeping some payments going for looking after the land, so we aren't wiped out by the big ones. And some honest advice, from someone like the college, not from a sales rep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Even if the robots do the work, somebody owns the fields, and it matters who. If it's all sold to companies, the villages empty out. That's what I'd worry about for the next lot of kids round here.

headlineQuote: Even if the robots do the work, somebody owns the fields, and it matters who.
portrait: Yusuf Young is 27 and works on his uncle Harun's beef and hay farm, Stonebridge, looking after about 120 suckler cows. He lives with his partner Amira, a vet's receptionist, keeps his calving records in a paper notebook and has never used AI tools. He takes the mild scenarios calmly, trusting his uncle's careful spending to shelter the small farm. The fast AGI picture alarms him because cheap robot-farmed beef could force a sale, and he'd pause the house deposit rather than retrain. With longer warning his worry shifts to the farm he expects to inherit and the conversation with his uncle he has never had.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because his uncle might have to sell the farm before they even understood what was happening.
whatWouldHelp: Government support for small family farms, such as continued payments for caring for the land, and honest advice from a college rather than a sales rep.
